recyclable.label: Recyclable
recyclable.description: Items that can be processed and reused as raw materials for new products.

organic.label: Organic / Wet Waste
organic.description: Biodegradable waste that can be composted or processed into organic fertilizer.

ewaste.label: E-Waste
ewaste.description: Electronic and electrical waste requiring specialized recycling to recover materials and prevent toxic contamination.

non_recyclable.label: Non-Recyclable
non_recyclable.description: Items that cannot be economically recycled and must be disposed of responsibly.

unknown.label: Unknown / Unidentified
unknown.description: The item could not be confidently identified. Please try again or classify manually.

items.disposalMethod: Place in dry waste / recyclable bin after rinsing and removing the cap.
preparation: Empty and rinse the bottle with water.
Remove the cap and label if possible.
Crush the bottle to save space.
Keep dry until collection.
items.specialNotes: PET bottles (marked with ♳ or number 1) are among the most recyclable plastics. Avoid bottles contaminated with chemicals or oils.

sources.name: Central Pollution Control Board - Plastic Waste Management

regionalRules.Mumbai: Place in blue dry-waste bin. BMC collects dry waste on alternate days.
regionalRules.Delhi: Segregate as dry waste. EDMC/SDMC/NDMC collect recyclables separately.
regionalRules.Bengaluru: Place in dry waste bin (white). BBMP collects dry waste daily.
regionalRules.Chennai: Segregate as recyclable dry waste. Corporation collects door-to-door.

items.disposalMethod: Flatten and place in dry waste / recyclable bin. Sell to local kabadiwala for recycling.
preparation: Remove any tape, staples, or packing material.
Flatten the box to save space.
Keep dry — wet cardboard is harder to recycle.
Remove any food residue.
warnings: Heavily greased or food-soiled cardboard (e.g., pizza boxes with oil) should go to organic/wet waste instead.
items.specialNotes: Clean cardboard is highly recyclable. The kabadiwala network in India is one of the most effective informal recycling systems in the world.

regionalRules.default: Sell to local kabadiwala or place in dry waste bin.

items.disposalMethod: Collect and place in dry waste bin or sell to kabadiwala.
preparation: Keep paper clean and dry.
Remove plastic covers or lamination.
Bundle newspapers together.
Separate glossy magazines from plain paper if possible.
warnings: Thermal paper (receipts), waxed paper, and heavily soiled paper are non-recyclable.
items.specialNotes: Paper can be recycled 5-7 times before fibers become too short. Shredded paper is harder to recycle.

regionalRules.default: Sell to local kabadiwala or place in dry waste collection.

items.disposalMethod: Rinse and place in dry waste bin. Aluminium cans have high recycling value.
preparation: Empty and rinse the can.
Remove any paper labels if easy.
Crush if possible to save space.
Do not mix with hazardous chemical containers.
warnings: Aerosol cans should be fully emptied before disposal. Never puncture aerosol cans.
items.specialNotes: Aluminium is infinitely recyclable without quality loss. Recycling aluminium uses 95% less energy than producing new aluminium.

regionalRules.default: Sell to kabadiwala or place in dry waste bin.

items.disposalMethod: Rinse and place in dry waste bin carefully. Handle with care to avoid breakage.
preparation: Rinse the bottle or jar.
Remove metal caps and lids (recycle separately).
Handle carefully to avoid breakage.
Wrap broken glass in newspaper before disposal.
warnings: Broken glass should be wrapped in newspaper and labeled 'BROKEN GLASS' for handler safety.
items.specialNotes: Glass is 100% recyclable and can be recycled endlessly without loss of quality. However, glass recycling infrastructure varies by city in India.

regionalRules.default: Sell to kabadiwala or place in dry waste bin.

items.disposalMethod: Clean and place in dry waste bin if the packaging material is recyclable.
preparation: Check for recycling symbols on the packaging.
Clean off any food residue.
Flatten to save space.
Separate different materials if mixed (e.g., plastic window on cardboard).
warnings: Multi-layer packaging (like chip packets, tetra packs) is difficult to recycle. Check local facilities.
items.specialNotes: Not all packaging is recyclable. Look for recycling symbols. Multi-layer packaging (MLP) requires specialized recycling facilities.

regionalRules.default: Place in dry waste bin. Multi-layer packaging may need specialized collection.

items.disposalMethod: Place in wet waste / organic bin. Ideal for composting.
preparation: Separate from any non-organic packaging.
Place directly in wet waste bin.
Can be used for home composting.
No need to rinse or clean.
items.specialNotes: Fruit peels are excellent for composting. Citrus peels may take longer to decompose. Consider home composting if available.

regionalRules.Mumbai: Place in green wet-waste bin. BMC collects daily.
regionalRules.Bengaluru: Place in green wet waste bin. BBMP mandates source segregation.
regionalRules.Delhi: Place in green wet waste bin.
regionalRules.Chennai: Place in wet waste bin for daily collection.

items.disposalMethod: Place in wet waste / organic bin. Excellent for composting.
preparation: Collect in a separate wet waste container.
Drain excess water if possible.
Do not mix with plastic bags.
Can be composted at home.
items.specialNotes: Vegetable scraps decompose quickly and are ideal for vermicomposting. Many Indian cities now mandate wet waste segregation.

regionalRules.default: Place in green/wet waste bin for municipal collection.

items.disposalMethod: Place in wet/organic waste bin or compost directly.
preparation: Collect in a biodegradable bag or directly in the bin.
Can be used as mulch in gardens.
Mix with other organic waste for composting.
Do not burn — open burning is banned in most Indian cities.
warnings: Do not burn leaves. Open burning causes air pollution and is prohibited under municipal and environmental regulations.
items.specialNotes: Dry leaves make excellent composting material when mixed with wet kitchen waste (brown + green composting).

regionalRules.default: Place in organic waste bin. Do not burn.

items.disposalMethod: Place in wet waste bin. Do not mix with dry waste or recyclables.
preparation: Remove any non-food items (plastic, foil, etc.).
Place in wet waste bin without plastic bags.
Drain excess liquids if possible.
Consider donating excess edible food to food banks.
items.specialNotes: India wastes approximately 68.7 million tonnes of food annually. Consider reducing food waste at the source.

sources.name: Ministry of Environment - Solid Waste Management Rules 2016

regionalRules.default: Place in green/wet waste bin for daily collection.

items.disposalMethod: Place in wet waste bin or use directly as garden fertilizer.
preparation: Remove from any non-biodegradable filter or packaging.
Can be added directly to compost or garden soil.
Tea bags may contain plastic — tear open and compost only the leaves.
Let cool before composting.
items.specialNotes: Coffee grounds are nitrogen-rich and excellent for composting. They can also deter certain garden pests.

regionalRules.default: Place in wet waste bin or compost at home.

items.disposalMethod: Do NOT dispose in regular waste. Take to an authorized e-waste collection centre or producer take-back programme.
preparation: Back up and erase all personal data.
Remove SIM card and memory card.
Keep charger and accessories for separate e-waste disposal.
Do not attempt to disassemble.
Check if the manufacturer offers a take-back programme.
warnings: Contains lithium batteries — do not burn, crush, or puncture.
Contains hazardous materials — improper disposal contaminates soil and groundwater.
Erase all personal data before disposal.
items.specialNotes: Under the E-Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2022), producers and manufacturers are responsible for collecting e-waste. Many brands offer take-back or exchange programmes.

regionalRules.default: Find an authorized e-waste dismantler/recycler listed on the CPCB website.

items.disposalMethod: Collect with other e-waste and dispose at an authorized e-waste collection point.
preparation: Bundle cables neatly.
Do not cut or strip cables.
Collect with other small e-waste items.
Drop off at an authorized collection point or e-waste drive.
warnings: Do not burn cables — the plastic coating releases toxic fumes.
items.specialNotes: Many electronics retailers and manufacturers accept old cables and chargers. Check for local e-waste collection drives.

regionalRules.default: Take to an authorized e-waste collection centre.

items.disposalMethod: Must be handled by authorized e-waste recyclers. Contains valuable and hazardous materials.
preparation: Do not attempt to extract components.
Handle carefully — edges can be sharp.
Store in a dry place until disposal.
Take to an authorized e-waste facility.
warnings: Contains lead, mercury, cadmium, and other hazardous substances.
Informal recycling of circuit boards is illegal and extremely hazardous.
Never burn circuit boards.
items.specialNotes: Circuit boards contain recoverable gold, silver, copper, and other valuable metals. Only authorized facilities should process them.

regionalRules.default: Take to CPCB-authorized e-waste dismantler or recycler.

items.disposalMethod: Do NOT throw in regular waste. Use designated battery collection points.
preparation: Tape the terminals of lithium batteries to prevent short circuits.
Do not store loose batteries together.
Keep away from heat and moisture.
Take to a battery collection point or e-waste centre.
warnings: Batteries contain corrosive and toxic chemicals.
Lithium batteries can catch fire if damaged — handle with care.
Never puncture, crush, or incinerate batteries.
Keep away from children.
items.specialNotes: Battery waste requires specialized handling under the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022. Many retail stores have battery drop-off bins.

regionalRules.default: Use battery drop-off bins at electronics stores or authorized collection centres.

items.disposalMethod: Single-use plastic bags are banned in India. Reuse if possible or place in dry waste.
preparation: Check thickness — bags below 75 microns are banned.
Reuse thicker bags as many times as possible.
Clean and dry before placing in dry waste.
Switch to cloth or jute bags.
warnings: Single-use plastic bags below 75 microns are banned under the Plastic Waste Management Amendment Rules 2021.
Do not burn plastic bags — releases toxic dioxins.
items.specialNotes: India banned single-use plastics in phases. As of 2022, carry bags must be at least 75 microns thick.

regionalRules.default: Avoid using single-use plastic bags. Use alternatives.

items.disposalMethod: Difficult to recycle. Place in dry waste bin. Avoid using styrofoam products.
preparation: Clean off any food residue.
Do not break into small pieces — creates microplastic pollution.
Place in dry waste bin.
Consider reusing for packaging if clean.
warnings: Styrofoam/thermocol is banned for food packaging in many Indian states and cities.
items.specialNotes: Expanded polystyrene (thermocol) is extremely difficult to recycle and persists in the environment for hundreds of years.

regionalRules.default: Place in dry waste. Check if locally banned.

cities.name: Mumbai
cities.segregationRules: Mandatory source segregation into wet waste (green bin) and dry waste (blue bin).
cities.notes: BMC has implemented mandatory waste segregation. Fines apply for non-compliance.

cities.name: Delhi
cities.segregationRules: Mandatory segregation into biodegradable (green), recyclable (blue), and domestic hazardous waste (red).
cities.notes: Delhi follows a three-bin segregation system.

cities.name: Bengaluru
cities.segregationRules: Mandatory segregation into wet waste (green), dry waste (white), and reject waste (red/black).
cities.collectionSchedule: Daily wet waste collection; dry waste on specific days.
cities.notes: BBMP pioneered source segregation in India. Strict enforcement with fines.

cities.name: Chennai
cities.segregationRules: Mandatory segregation into biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste.
cities.notes: GCC provides door-to-door waste collection across all zones.

cities.name: Pune
cities.segregationRules: Mandatory source segregation into wet and dry waste.
cities.notes: PMC has been a leader in waste management innovation in India.

cities.name: Hyderabad
cities.segregationRules: Mandatory segregation into wet waste and dry waste.

cities.name: Kolkata
cities.segregationRules: Segregation into biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste encouraged.
cities.notes: KMC is progressively implementing source segregation.

cities.name: Ahmedabad
cities.segregationRules: Mandatory wet and dry waste segregation.
cities.notes: AMC has implemented colour-coded bins across the city.

composting.title: Home Composting
composting.description: Convert kitchen waste into nutrient-rich compost at home.
steps: Get a compost bin or designate a composting area.
Add green waste (fruit peels, vegetable scraps) and brown waste (dry leaves, cardboard).
Maintain moisture — the pile should feel like a wrung-out sponge.
Turn the pile every 1-2 weeks for aeration.
Compost is ready in 2-3 months when it looks and smells like dark, crumbly soil.

ewasteDisposal.title: E-Waste Disposal in India
ewasteDisposal.description: Under the E-Waste Management Rules 2016, producers, consumers, and recyclers have specific responsibilities.
steps: Identify your nearest authorized e-waste collection centre on the CPCB website.
Check if the manufacturer offers a take-back programme.
Many cities hold periodic e-waste collection drives.
Never sell e-waste to informal / unauthorized recyclers.
Erase personal data from all electronic devices before disposal.

reducePlastic.title: Reducing Plastic Waste
reducePlastic.description: Simple steps to minimize plastic waste in daily life.
steps: Avoid single-use plastic cutlery and straws.
Choose products with minimal or recyclable packaging.
Refuse unnecessary plastic bags at shops.
